# Robeco Quant team publishes new research paper

#### Guido Baltussen, Bart Van Vliet and Pim Van Vliet at Robeco, in collaboration with Erasmus University of Rotterdam, have published a new research paper, titled: The Cross-Section of Stock Returns before 1926 (and beyond).

This new paper studies a cross section of stock returns using a novel constructed database of U.S. stocks covering 61 years of additional and independent data. The database contains data on stock prices, dividends and hand-collected market capitalizations for 1,488 major stocks between 1866-1926. Results over this ‘pre-CRSP’ era reveal a flat relation between market beta and returns, an insignificant size premium, and significant momentum, value and low-risk premiums that are of similar size over the post-1926 period. Overall, stock characteristics can explain over 25% of variation in stock returns. Further, recent machine learning methods are successful in predicting cross-sectional returns out-of-sample. These results show strong out-of-sample robustness of traditional factor models and novel machine learning methods.

Highlights:

- For this large project, the Robeco Quant team, in collaboration with Erasmus University of Rotterdam, built up a hand-collected database of American stocks between 1866 and 1926
- These stocks have been used to study factor premiums in an independent sample, in order to gain more insight into their expected performance. In addition, machine learning methods have been applied

Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. These improvements translate into lower relative errors on portfolio volatility and kurtosis, and into lower out-of-sample volatility and kurtosis when the portfolio objective penalizes both variance and the fourth moment.

## Abstract

We develop a rotation-invariant neural network that provides the global minimum-variance portfolio by jointly learning how to lag-transform historical returns and marginal volatilities and how to regularise the eigenvalues of large equity covariance matrices. This explicit mathematical mapping offers clear interpretability of each module's role, so the model cannot be regarded as a pure black box. Furthermore, although the model is trained end-to-end to produce an unconstrained minimum-variance portfolio, we show that its learned covariance representation can be used in general optimizers under long-only constraints with virtually no loss in its performance advantage over competing estimators. exa-lite.snippet:
###### Abstract

Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. These improvements translate into lower relative errors on portfolio volatility and kurtosis, and into lower out-of-sample volatility and kurtosis when the portfolio objective penalizes both variance and the fourth moment.

Mr. Bogle’s model is pretty simple:

> Expected returns (nominal, annualized over the next 10 years) = Starting Dividend Yield + Earnings Growth rate + Percentage change (annualized) in the P/E multiple.

_By Victor Haghani and James White[1](https://elmwealth.com/bogleheads/#easy-footnote-bottom-1-11791)_  
ESTIMATED READING TIME: 6 min.

“Bogleheads” are DIY investors who are passionate about index investing. They gather each year to share ideas about sensible investing, and to celebrate the life and contributions of John Bogle, the founder of Vanguard and arguably the person who has done more than anyone to improve investor welfare. Victor was very pleased to attend their recent annual conference in Minneapolis, and do a Q&A session with Morningstar’s Christine Benz. There were also about a dozen authors of excellent personal finance books and blogs who gave presentations, including Christine Benz, Rick Ferri, William Bernstein, Allan Roth, Mike Piper, Jackie Cummings Koski, Karsten Jeske and Sarah-Catherine Gutierrez. Victor thoroughly enjoyed the experience, and hopes he’ll be invited back to next year’s conference in Austin!

We agree 100% with almost everything discussed over the course of the three-day conference. However, one area where we noticed our opinions diverge from the Boglehead consensus view was on asset allocation. Beta measures a stock's price [volatility](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/v/volatility.asp) relative to the overall market. It is an important factor for investors to check when they want to choose a stock that matches their tolerance for risk.

By definition, the market, such as the S&P 500, has a beta of 1.0. Every stock has a beta that indicates how widely its price swings in comparison with the market as a whole. keenable.title: Nonlinear Shrinkage for Higher Moments Estimation in Large Portfolios
keenable.snippet: Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. These improvements translate into lower relative errors on portfolio volatility and kurtosis, and into lower out-of-sample volatility and kurtosis when the portfolio objective penalizes both variance and the fourth moment.

which firm characteristics determine the factor loadings and economic conditions de-
termine the expected factors. Both relations are estimated nonparametrically with

keenable.title: Do econophysics-inspired inputs improve neural covariance forecasting? A leakage-free walk-forward study of intraday DJIA data
keenable.snippet: Tools from econophysics—random matrix theory (RMT), Tsallis q-Gaussian tails, Hawkes self-excitation and diffusion-based regularisation—are often proposed as ingredients for financial risk models, but their incremental value over strong, simple benchmarks is rarely measured under strict temporal controls. We build a Physics-Inspired Neural Covariance model (PINC) that forecasts the next-day realised covariance matrix of the 29 Dow Jones constituents from 1-min data (545 trading days, 2012–2015). The network uses RMT-cleaned correlations, a Tsallis tail index and Hawkes intensities as inputs, and may add a Fokker–Planck-inspired regulariser whose weight is chosen on validation data only. It is compared with sample, Ledoit–Wolf, RMT and extreme-value covariances, a HAR-RV model, an LSTM and a plain network of equal capacity, in a nested walk-forward design with 11 folds, 231 out-of-sample days and 3 seeds, verified by look-ahead and bit-identical leakage tests. The regulariser was rejected on validation in every fold, so PINC and the plain network coincide. The neural forecasts beat static estimators (Holm-adjusted p<0.001) but not HAR-RV (p=0.151) or the LSTM (p=0.528); removing the RMT, Tsallis or Hawkes inputs has no detectable effect; and minimum-variance portfolios show no significant Sharpe-ratio gain after costs. keenable.title: Uncertainty-Adjusted Sorting for Asset Pricing with Machine Learning
keenable.snippet: Machine learning is central to empirical asset pricing, but portfolio construction still relies on point predictions and largely ignores asset-specific estimation uncertainty. octen.snippet: This paper develops a large-scale inference approach for the regularization of stock return covariance matrices. The framework allows for the presence of heavy tails and multivariate GARCH-type effects of unknown form among the stock returns. This adaptive thresholding is achieved through sign-based Monte Carlo resampling within multiple testing procedures, controlling either the traditional familywise error rate, a generalized familywise error rate, or the false discovery proportion. Compared to alternative estimators, this new regularization method demonstrates strong performance in simulation experiments and real portfolio optimization.

## Abstract

This paper presents how the use of a cleaned and robust covariance matrix estimate can improve significantly the overall performance of maximum variety and minimum variance portfolios. We assume that the asset returns are modelled through a multi-factor model where the error term is a multivariate and correlated elliptical symmetric noise extending the classical Gaussian assumptions. ## Shrinkage Covariance Models

## 1. Why a Risk Model Needs Shrinkage

A covariance matrix is the engine room of almost every market risk number for an equity book. Parametric VaR, risk decomposition, hedge ratios, tracking error and the optimiser that builds a minimum-risk portfolio all read from the same table of variances and covariances. The trouble is that the table is estimated, and the number of things to estimate grows much faster than the data. Fifty stocks need 1,275 distinct variances and covariances. Two years of daily data gives each stock about 500 observations, which sounds generous until you notice that every one of those 1,275 entries carries its own sampling error, and that the errors do not cancel when the matrix is used.

They do the opposite. An optimiser hunts for combinations of assets that the matrix says are low risk, and the combinations that look lowest are disproportionately the ones where estimation error happened to make a covariance too small. The portfolio is then riskier than the model said, and the model's risk forecast for it is too low. The risk team gets hit twice: a worse portfolio and an optimistic report about it.

Shrinkage covariance models attack both problems. The general statistics of shrinkage are covered in Shrinkage Estimation of Covariance Matrices, and the estimator itself in Ledoit-Wolf Covariance Estimation. This post looks at shrinkage as a *risk model*: which target to pick, how hard to shrink, how much out-of-sample risk it saves on a minimum-variance portfolio, and how much of the gap between predicted and realised risk it closes. The last answer is the one most often overstated.

## Ledoit-Wolf Covariance Estimation

Every portfolio optimiser needs a covariance matrix, and the one you estimate from history is noisy. Shrinkage fixes much of that noise by blending the noisy matrix with a simple, stable one. The open question is *how much* to blend. Olivier Ledoit and Michael Wolf answered it with a formula you can compute from the data alone, and in three papers (2003 and twice in 2004) they gave three versions of it. This post computes all three by hand on one illustrative 12-stock sample, checks the most popular one against the scikit-learn library, and then asks the question practitioners rarely get to ask: over 1,000 simulated histories where we know the true matrix, how close does the formula land to the best possible answer?

A **covariance matrix** is a table that holds every asset's **variance** (how much its return swings around its average) on the diagonal and every pair's **covariance** (how much two returns swing together) off the diagonal. In 1952 Harry Markowitz turned \"do not put all your eggs in one basket\" into mathematics, and in 1990 it won him the Nobel prize. Oracle Approximating Shrinkage (OAS) explained for beginners: the Gaussian oracle formula, OAS computed by hand on 12 stocks, a 1,000-sample race against Ledoit-Wolf, and why fat tails make OAS under-shrink.

## Oracle Approximating Shrinkage

Every minimum-variance portfolio is only as good as the covariance matrix fed into it, and every covariance matrix you can compute is an estimate from a short, noisy history. Shrinkage cleans that estimate by blending it with a simple target. The hard question is *how much* to blend. Oracle Approximating Shrinkage (OAS) answers it with one closed-form number. This post explains where that number comes from, computes it by hand, and then races it against Ledoit-Wolf and against the true answer on data where the truth is known.

## 1. What an Oracle Is: Shrinkage in Plain English

A **covariance matrix** is a table with one row and one column per stock. The diagonal holds each stock's **variance** (the average squared deviation of its return from its mean); every off-diagonal cell holds a **covariance**, which says how two stocks move together. Covariance Matrices in Portfolio Optimization shows how an optimiser uses it.

The **sample covariance matrix** estimated from, say, 60 months of returns contains real structure plus noise. An optimiser cannot tell the two apart, so it bets heavily on the noise. **Shrinkage** replaces the sample matrix by a weighted average of the sample and a dull, stable **target**. The weight on the target is the **shrinkage intensity**, written ρ (rho), a number between 0 (trust the sample fully) and 1 (ignore the data, use the target). Shrinkage Estimation of Covariance Matrices compares four targets; here we use the simplest one throughout.

## Factor-Based Covariance Estimation

## 1. Why Estimate a Covariance Matrix Through Factors

A portfolio’s risk depends on how its holdings move together. That information sits in the **covariance matrix**: a table with one row and one column per stock, where each diagonal entry is a stock’s *variance* (the average squared distance of its return from its mean) and each off-diagonal entry is a *covariance* (how strongly two stocks move together, in the same squared units). ## Positive Semi-Definite Covariance Matrices

A covariance matrix makes one promise that every risk number downstream relies on: whatever portfolio you build from its assets, the matrix will never tell you that portfolio has *negative* variance. That promise has a technical name, **positive semi-definite** (PSD), and a covariance estimated from one complete table of returns always keeps it. The trouble starts when the history is ragged — some stocks list later, some have missing months — and each pair of stocks is estimated on whatever months the two happen to share. This post builds exactly that situation on an example universe whose true covariance we know, breaks the matrix, repairs it three ways, and then asks the question that matters to a portfolio manager: does the repaired matrix build a good portfolio?

## 1. What Positive Semi-Definite Promises a Portfolio

Start with the pieces. A **weight** wi is the fraction of the portfolio in asset i (negative for a short). A **variance** σi2 measures how widely an asset's return swings around its average; its square root is the volatility. A **covariance** σij measures whether two assets tend to be above their averages at the same time; divide it by both volatilities and you get the **correlation** ρij, which lives between −1 and +1. The **covariance matrix** Σ is the grid of all of these, with variances on the diagonal. The portfolio's variance is the sum over every pair:

*σp2 = ∑i ∑j wi wj σij*

## Principal Component Analysis for Portfolio Optimization

Principal component analysis (PCA) is usually taught as a way to *describe* a covariance matrix: find the few patterns that explain most of the movement. This post uses it as a tool for *optimising* a portfolio. We take 300 stocks, estimate how they move together from a few years of data, clean that estimate with a rule from random matrix theory, and then ask the only question that matters to a portfolio builder: does the cleaned estimate lead to a portfolio that is genuinely less risky? Because our stocks are simulated from a known model, we can answer with the true risk, not the estimated one.

## 1. Why PCA Belongs Inside the Optimiser

A **weight** is the share of the portfolio held in one stock, and the weights add up to 100%. The **variance** of a return is the average squared distance from its mean; its square root is the **volatility**, the usual measure of risk. The **covariance** between two stocks measures how they move together, and the table of every variance and covariance is the **covariance matrix**, written Σ (capital sigma). The simplest optimised portfolio, the global minimum-variance (GMV) portfolio, picks the weights that give the lowest possible variance. It needs no forecast of returns at all, only Σ, which makes it the cleanest test of a covariance estimate.

The trouble is size. With 300 stocks, Σ has 45,150 distinct entries. Ten years of monthly data supply 36,000 numbers. You are estimating more unknowns than you have observations, and an optimiser treats every estimation error as a real opportunity: it piles into combinations of stocks that *happened* to look calm.

Most writing about equity risk looks at one component at a time: how to estimate a beta, how to shrink a covariance matrix, how to backtest a VaR number. Each piece makes sense on its own. A risk manager, though, never gets to use one piece on its own. A bank's equity desk needs a single machine that takes in prices every evening and produces a VaR, an expected shortfall, a set of stress losses and a record of how well yesterday's numbers held up. Every stage of that machine feeds the next, so an error at the start flows through to the end.

## 1. Why Revisit a Theory From 1952?

Harry Markowitz published *Portfolio Selection* in 1952. It won a Nobel Prize, it built an industry, and it still occupies the opening chapters of the FRM and CFA curricula. It is also, in its literal form, wrong in ways that practitioners discovered almost immediately and have spent seventy years patching.

That combination — foundational and broken — is exactly why it is worth returning to. If you want the mechanics from scratch, we have already covered them in Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT) Explained and in Markowitz Efficient Frontier Explained. This article assumes you have that and asks a harder question: **which parts of MPT survive contact with real markets, which parts fail, and what replaced the failing parts?**

The answer matters commercially, not just academically. Every strategic asset allocation committee, every risk-parity fund, every robo-adviser's glide path, and every regulatory capital model with a correlation matrix inside it is a descendant of Markowitz. When the theory misbehaves, real portfolios misbehave. In 2008 and again in March 2020, diversified portfolios built on historical covariance matrices lost far more than their models said was plausible — not because the mathematics was miscoded, but because the inputs were fiction.

## What Monte Carlo simulation actually does

The term "Monte Carlo" refers to a broad class of computational methods that use repeated random sampling to obtain numerical results — a name coined by physicists Stanislaw Ulam and Nicholas Metropolis in 1949, borrowed from the famous casino, since the method depends on chance the way roulette does. In the context of portfolio planning, the methodology is conceptually direct: define a return distribution and covariance structure for the asset classes in the portfolio, draw random correlated return sequences for each period across a chosen time horizon, and compute the resulting portfolio value. Repeat this process thousands of times — typically 10,000 paths is standard — and collect the distribution of terminal outcomes.

The return distributions can be constructed in two principal ways. The first is parametric: assume that returns follow a known distribution (most commonly normal, or Gaussian) characterised by a mean and covariance matrix estimated from historical data or set as forward-looking assumptions. The second is historical bootstrapping: draw actual historical return sequences at random, with replacement, preserving the correlation structure across asset classes in each sampled period. Each approach has trade-offs, covered in full in the methods comparison section below.

The output of 10,000 simulated paths is visualised as a fan chart: a band of possible portfolio trajectories that narrows near inception (all paths start from the same point) and widens with time as the paths diverge. The fan is shaded to show percentile bands — the 10th through 90th percentile corridor, the median line, and typically the 25th and 75th percentile inner band. ultimate.title: Nonlinear Shrinkage for Higher Moments Estimation in Large Portfolios
ultimate.snippet: Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. ultimate.title: End-to-End Large Portfolio Optimization for Variance Minimization with Neural Networks through Covariance Cleaning
ultimate.snippet:
We develop a rotation-invariant neural network that provides the global minimum-variance portfolio by jointly learning how to lag-transform historical returns and how to regularise both the eigenvalues and the marginal volatilities of large equity covariance matrices. This explicit mathematical mapping offers clear interpretability of each module’s role, so the model cannot be regarded as a pure black-box. The architecture mirrors the analytical form of the global minimum-variance solution yet remains agnostic to dimension, so a single model can be calibrated on panels of a few hundred stocks and applied, without retraining, to one thousand US equities—a cross-sectional jump that demonstrates robust out-of-sample generalisation. The loss function is the future realized minimum portfolio variance and is optimized end-to-end on real daily returns. In out-of-sample tests from January 2000 to December 2024 the estimator delivers systematically lower realised volatility, smaller maximum drawdowns, and higher Sharpe ratios than the best analytical competitors, including state-of-the-art non-linear shrinkage. ultimate.snippet: Tools from econophysics—random matrix theory (RMT), Tsallis q-Gaussian tails, Hawkes self-excitation and diffusion-based regularisation—are often proposed as ingredients for financial risk models, but their incremental value over strong, simple benchmarks is rarely measured under strict temporal controls. We build a Physics-Inspired Neural Covariance model (PINC) that forecasts the next-day realised covariance matrix of the 29 Dow Jones constituents from 1-min data (545 trading days, 2012–2015). The network uses RMT-cleaned correlations, a Tsallis tail index and Hawkes intensities as inputs, and may add a Fokker–Planck-inspired regulariser whose weight is chosen on validation data only. It is compared with sample, Ledoit–Wolf, RMT and extreme-value covariances, a HAR-RV model, an LSTM and a plain network of equal capacity, in a nested walk-forward design with 11 folds, 231 out-of-sample days and 3 seeds, verified by look-ahead and bit-identical leakage tests. The regulariser was rejected on validation in every fold, so PINC and the plain network coincide. The neural forecasts beat static estimators (Holm-adjusted p<0.001) but not HAR-RV (p=0.151) or the LSTM (p=0.528); removing the RMT, Tsallis or Hawkes inputs has no detectable effect; and minimum-variance portfolios show no significant Sharpe-ratio gain after costs.
